hero.intro: An Angular library that binds a UI action to the lifecycle of its HTTP request. Buttons stay disabled while the request is pending and re-enable when it completes, with no manual loading flags.

install.title: Install
install.note: Requires Angular v22 or newer. Uses standalone APIs, functional HTTP interceptors and signals.

problem.intro: A common category of front-end bugs comes from the gap between a UI action and the HTTP request it triggers. The user clicks; the request is in flight; the button is still enabled; the user clicks again. Two identical requests reach the server. The application state diverges.

symptoms.title: Symptoms
symptoms.list:
• Duplicate POST/PUT/DELETE requests from repeated clicks.
  • Duplicate form submissions racing to update the same record.
  • Ad hoc loading booleans spread across every component that talks to the network.
  • Loading flags that stay true forever when an error path forgets to reset them.
  • Disabled-state logic drifting out of sync with the actual request lifecycle.

naive.title: The naive approach
naive.text: The typical fix is a component-level boolean toggled around each request. It works, but it is repetitive, error-prone on error paths, and does not survive concurrent calls with the same intent.

withLibrary.title: With ngx-request-lock
withLibrary.text: The directive owns the lock. The request carries a lock id in its HttpContext. A functional interceptor updates a shared signal-backed service; the directive reads that signal and re-enables the button when the request settles. No component-level booleans, no manual reset in error handlers.

scope.title: What this library is not
scope.list:
• It does not cancel or debounce requests.
  • It does not replace HTTP-level idempotency on the server.
  • It does not implement a global spinner or toast system.

architecture.intro: The library is composed of four small pieces that communicate through Angular's own primitives: an HttpContextToken, a functional HttpInterceptorFn, a signal-backed service, and a directive. No external state container, no observable orchestration in user code.

buildingBlocks.title: Building blocks
buildingBlocks.list:
• REQUEST_LOCK_ID — an HttpContextToken<string | null> that tags a request with a lock identifier.
  • createRequestLockContext(id) — builds the HttpContext to attach to the request.
  • requestLockInterceptor — a functional interceptor that reads the id from the context and drives the service.
  • RequestLockService — a singleton service holding a reference-counted map of pending requests, exposed as a Signal<boolean> per id via isPending(id).
  • RequestLockDirective ([ngxRequestLock]) — generates a UUID as requestId, disables the host button on click, and unblocks when the matching signal settles.
  • provideRequestLock() — registers provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([requestLockInterceptor])) in one call.

dataFlow.title: Data flow
dataFlow.steps:
• The user clicks the host element. The directive stores isBlocked = true and sets the disabled attribute on the nearest <button>.
  • The consumer sends an HTTP request whose HttpContext carries the directive's requestId via createRequestLockContext(id).
  • requestLockInterceptor reads REQUEST_LOCK_ID from the context. If present, it calls RequestLockService.start(id) and pipes the response through finalize(() => end(id)).
  • The service updates its internal signal<Record<string, number>>. An effect inside the directive observes isPending(id) and calls unblock() when the signal transitions from true back to false.
  • The button is re-enabled. Two safety timeouts also unblock: at 500ms if no pending state was ever observed, and at 10s unconditionally.

architecture.httpContextNote: HttpContext is local. HttpContext is Angular client-side metadata attached to a request instance. It is not serialized to headers, body, or query string, and never reaches the server.

refCount.title: Reference-counted state
refCount.text: RequestLockService increments a counter per id on start and decrements on end. Multiple concurrent requests can share the same lock id and only the last end flips isPending(id) back to false.
refCount.note: RequestLockService.isPending(id) returns a new computed on every call. Store the returned signal in a field if you read it repeatedly in the same component.

examples.intro: Every example below wires RequestLockDirective to a real HTTP call. The button stays blocked while the request tagged with its requestId is pending, and is re-enabled automatically when the request settles — success or error. No loading boolean, no manual reset in error handlers.
examples.tipConfig: All snippets assume provideRequestLock() is registered in app.config.ts. See the Installation page.

basic.title: Basic use case
basic.text: The minimum viable wiring: a button, the directive, a template reference exported as requestLock, and one HTTP request whose HttpContext carries the lock id via createRequestLockContext(id).
basic.bullets:
• #lock="requestLock" exposes the directive instance to the template.
  • lock.requestId is a stable UUID generated once per directive instance.
  • The button is disabled from the click until the interceptor sees the request settle.

crud.title: Save, delete, form examples
crud.text: The pattern is identical for every non-idempotent action. The only thing that changes is the HTTP verb and the payload; the directive, the exported reference and the context helper stay the same.

examples.formNote: The submit button in the form example combines ngxRequestLock with [disabled]="form.invalid". The directive re-applies its own disabled only while the request is pending; when it re-enables the button, form validity takes over again.

custom.title: Custom directive: loading animation
custom.text: The library keeps the visual side deliberately empty: RequestLockDirective only toggles the native disabled attribute on the nearest button. To show a spinner or a custom animation, extend the directive in your own app and override the setBlockStatus extension point.
custom.info: This directive lives in the docs app under src/app/pages/examples/loading-request-lock.directive.ts. It is deliberately separate from the library so ngx-request-lock stays styling-agnostic.
custom.usageText: Consume it exactly like the base directive; only the selector and the exported name change.
custom.warning: The base directive is not final, but its constructor injections and the @HostListener('click') live on the parent class. Do not shadow onClick and do not re-declare the click host binding in the subclass — override only setBlockStatus.

why.title: Why this matters in consumer projects
why.intro: The same three characters — ngxRequestLock, #lock, createRequestLockContext — cover every action-triggered HTTP call in an application. That uniformity is the whole point:
why.bullets:
• No per-component boilerplate. No loading boolean, no finalize in user code, no manual reset in error handlers.
  • Correctness on error paths. The button is re-enabled through the interceptor's finalize, so a thrown error, a 5xx response, or a cancelled subscription all leave the UI consistent.
  • Concurrent requests share a lock. The service reference-counts pending requests per id, so a component that fires several requests under the same requestId only unblocks when all of them settle.
  • Styling stays in the app. The library ships zero CSS; the custom directive above shows the exact seam where visual behavior belongs.
  • Angular-native surface. HttpContext, functional interceptors, signals — no external state container, no RxJS orchestration in user code.
